source.title: Memorization and Generalization in Neural Code Intelligence Models
source.citation: Md Rafiqul Islam Rabin et al., 2021
source.authors: Md Rafiqul Islam Rabin; Aftab Hussain; Mohammad Amin Alipour; Vincent J. Hellendoorn

record.tranche_reason: Tests noise-driven memorization in code-intelligence models, extending the label-noise experiments to code tasks and models.
record.gate_note: The paper tests output noise by randomly replacing target labels and reports training performance. It also reports input-noise experiments, but those use task-specific code transformations rather than shuffled or Gaussian inputs. Values described only in figures are recorded as figure only. Cited image-model results are not extracted as this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study extends label-corruption experiments to neural code models and reports training fit and clean-evaluation performance. Its output-noise results bear on V1 and V4, and its comparison of training trajectories bears on part of V2. CodeSearch's complete binary-label inversion is not a completely random labeling.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that models with excessive parameter capacity can readily memorize noisy code datasets, and that confidence and other training diagnostics may reveal memorization beyond training-versus-test comparisons. They also report substantial model and task differences; they do not demonstrate perfect random-label fitting by every model.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts the label-noise framework to code tasks and code-specific models; uses 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% output noise, with task-specific label substitutions. MethodName uses prior training configurations with a smaller batch size; other tasks mostly use default configurations with batch-size and sequence-length adjustments.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by model capacity, model family, dataset, task, noise level and task-specific noise construction.

fits_no_version.finding: CodeBERT CodeSearch reaches similar training accuracy with all binary labels inverted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A pretrained code model can learn a consistently reversed binary classification target.

fits_no_version.finding: Prediction confidence, loss inequality and adversarial sensitivity change with noise, with model-dependent exceptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise changes confidence and training diagnostics in neural code models; these diagnostics do not directly establish perfect memorization or clean-before-noise learning.

record.peer_reviewed: Information and Software Technology, IST Journal 2022, Elsevier
record.problems: Several result values are presented only in figures; no exact metric values are stated in the prose. Authors note that results may vary with randomization, repeated runs were performed for output noise, and default model capacities affect behavior. The study does not establish chance-level test error for fully randomized labels.
record.rows_left_out: No additional output-noise model-condition results were omitted. Input-noise results are task-specific transformations (such as statement deletion, identity cues and repair-information injection), not shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel or Gaussian-noise inputs, so they do not bear on V3.

untested.parts: Chance-level test error is not established. Near-zero exact-label training error is not established for Code2Vec by the supplied prose or readable figure values.
No convergence-time ratio to a common near-zero-error criterion is reported; progressive slowing with increasing corruption is not established.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, Gaussian-noise, or comparably unstructured-input experiment.
Chance-level evaluation endpoints and simultaneous perfect training fit throughout the corruption sweep are not established.
No controlled comparison of weight decay, dropout, augmentation, or their removal.
No separate tracking of clean and corrupted examples demonstrating shared patterns being learned before noisy labels. Confidence and aggregate loss-spread differences do not establish that ordering.

missing.what: A separate Code2Vec trajectory-comparison row capturing the authors' statement that most noisy curves follow nearly identical trajectories.

Training and clean-test performance across intermediate corruption levels, separated by model and dataset. Despite rows_left_out claiming completeness, the record contains only full-noise MethodName rows and omits the reported corruption-response trends.
VarMisuse repair accuracy and lower-corruption localization results, including clean held-out performance. Figure 4 contains these results, which rows_left_out does not identify as omitted.
Code-to-Text training and clean-validation results at 25%, 50% and 75% corruption, plus the validation trend at full corruption.

CodeSearch at 50% randomly selected label flips, which tests random-label fitting more directly than deterministic 100% inversion. Extract its training and validation accuracy if the curves become readable.

record.verdict_notes: Assessment uses only the supplied text. The extracted figures contain axes and legends but no readable curve coordinates. Equal clean/noisy performance therefore cannot establish near-zero training error. Random-label experiments remain relevant despite deliberately corrupting labels: the measured behavior is whether ordinary training fits those targets.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test image-classification networks or establish that test error is at chance; tested code tasks use randomly substituted task labels.
Does not test a common classification measure across models or establish a steadily rising test error to chance as corruption increases.

rows.subject: Code2Vec (Java-Top10)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with output noise replacing selected target labels with different randomly chosen available labels.
rows.note: Authors say Code2Vec training performance converges to nearly the same point in original and noisy settings; they attribute this to ample capacity for memorization.
rows.check: Similar final training F1 across noise levels establishes noise tolerance, but the supplied figure text contains no readable curve values establishing zero or near-zero training error. Subtoken F1 also does not directly report exact-label error.

rows.subject: Code2Vec (Java-Small)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with output noise replacing selected target labels with different randomly chosen available labels.
rows.note: Authors describe Code2Vec training performance as converging to nearly the same point in original and noisy settings.
rows.check: Convergence near the clean-data baseline does not establish perfect fitting; neither baseline nor noisy endpoint can be read from the supplied figure text. Subtoken F1 is not exact-label accuracy.

rows.subject: Code2Vec (Java-Med)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with output noise replacing selected target labels with different randomly chosen available labels.
rows.note: Authors describe Code2Vec training performance as converging to nearly the same point in original and noisy settings.
rows.check: Near-equal training performance does not establish near-zero error. Curve values are unavailable, and training stops at 20 epochs because of the time budget.

rows.subject: Code2Seq (Java-Top10)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with output noise replacing selected target labels with different randomly chosen available labels.
rows.note: Authors say Code2Seq struggles more with memorization and is unable to fit noisy training data perfectly.
rows.check: The prose explicitly reports incomplete noisy-data fitting. Preserve that qualitative result without inventing an endpoint.

rows.subject: Code2Seq (Java-Small)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with output noise replacing selected target labels with different randomly chosen available labels.
rows.note: Authors say Code2Seq struggles more with memorization and is unable to fit noisy training data perfectly.
rows.check: The prose explicitly reports incomplete noisy-data fitting; exact training F1 is unavailable.

rows.subject: Code2Seq (Java-Med)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with output noise replacing selected target labels with different randomly chosen available labels.
rows.note: Authors say Code2Seq struggles more with memorization and is unable to fit noisy training data perfectly.
rows.check: The prose reports incomplete fitting within the tested budget, which is only 20 epochs for Java-Med.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Trained on VarMisuse data with output noise changing labels and associated localization/repair targets.
rows.note: Authors state VarMisuse models fail to learn bug localization almost completely at noise levels of 75% and above, converging to marking every sample bug-free.
rows.check: The localization failure is explicit. Split 75% and 100% conditions: only 100% addresses V1's full-corruption endpoint. Corruption inverts bug status and randomizes locations for formerly correct samples; it is not independent randomization of every output component. Figure 4 uses training steps, not 50 full epochs.

rows.subject: GGNN
rows.operation_detail: Trained on VarMisuse data with output noise changing labels and associated localization/repair targets.
rows.note: Authors state VarMisuse models fail to learn bug localization almost completely at noise levels of 75% and above, converging to marking every sample bug-free.
rows.check: Split 75% and 100% conditions. Preserve the explicit localization failure and describe the structured corruption: bug-status inversion plus random locations for formerly correct samples. Figure 4 reports steps.

rows.subject: Great
rows.operation_detail: Trained on VarMisuse data with output noise changing labels and associated localization/repair targets.
rows.note: Authors state VarMisuse models fail to learn bug localization almost completely at noise levels of 75% and above, converging to marking every sample bug-free.
rows.check: Split 75% and 100% conditions. The failure concerns localization under structured output corruption, not independently randomized values for all output components. Figure 4 reports steps.

rows.subject: CodeBERT
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned with output noise replacing selected target docstrings with different randomly chosen docstrings.
rows.note: Authors say training is significantly impaired at 100% noise in this task.
rows.check: Significantly impaired training does not establish an absence of learning beyond baseline. The text supports incomplete fitting; BLEU endpoints and exact-output error are unavailable.

rows.subject: CodeBERT
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned with output noise flipping selected positive and negative labels.
rows.note: Authors say training accuracy on original and noisy sets converges toward the same point.
rows.check: At 100% corruption every binary label is inverted deterministically. The original predictive relationship remains learnable with its output reversed, so this condition cannot establish fitting completely random labels or V4's random-noise endpoint.

relationships.condition: Code2Seq on Java-Top10, Java-Small and Java-Med under full output corruption
relationships.reason: R4–R6 report that noisy training data are not fitted perfectly within the tested budgets.
relationships.display_finding: Code2Seq failed to fit the corrupted training outputs perfectly within the tested budgets across all three datasets.

relation.reason: Its own experiments measure noisy-output fitting, performance across corruption fractions and training trajectories.

tranche.reason: Adapts label-corruption experiments to code intelligence tasks and reports training and clean-evaluation outcomes in this new setting.

source_check.notes: Exact training endpoints remain figure-only; F1 and smoothed BLEU-4 do not directly establish exact-output training error. R7–R9 combine 75% and 100% corruption, but only 100% addresses V1’s full-corruption endpoint; the qualitative Code2Vec V2 result lacks a dedicated row.

reader_labels.reason: Training performance remains nearly the same under full output noise for these settings (R1–R3, R11). The paper does not establish chance-level test error.
